deep.reconstruction:
The page has two power-series inversions of Barker's equation for parabolic motion, plus a numerical check of the first one.

(A) Direct inversion. Gauss sets 2 tan(v/2) + (2/3) tan^3(v/2) = p, i.e. Barker's equation tau + tau^3/3 = p/2 with tau = tan(v/2). He inverts it to
v = p - p^3/6 + 13/240 p^5 - 43/2016 p^7 + 191/20736 p^9 - 479/114048 p^11 + ...
The coefficients are written in closed form twice (top of page and bottom line):
coefficient of p^(2n+1) = (-1)^n / ((2n+1) 4^n) * Sum_{k=0..n} C(2n+k, k) 3^(-k).
The top version writes C(2n+k,k)/3^k as (2n+1)(2n+2)...(2n+k)/(3*6*...*3k). Examples: 1/(3*4)*(1+3/3) = 1/6; 1/(5*16)*(1+5/3+5*6/(3*6)) = 13/240.
[Derivation, mine:] write t = p*psi(t) with psi = 1/(2(1+t^2/3)) and H = 2 arctan t. Lagrange-Burmann gives [p^m]H = (1/m)[t^(m-1)] 2(1+t^2)^(-1) (2(1+t^2/3))^(-m). This yields exactly that sum. It is the method of the bundle's namesake, Lagrange.

(B) Inversion near v = 180 deg. Gauss sets 1/tan(w/2) + 1/(3 tan^3(w/2)) = 8/(3q^3). This is Barker's equation with cot in place of tan, so the true anomaly is v = 180 deg - w, for large mean-anomaly parameter M = 8/(3q^3).
- With theta = tan(w/2) this becomes 8 theta^3 = q^3 + 3 q^3 theta^2. Putting q = 2r gives theta^3 = r^3(1 + 3 theta^2).
- He tried the substitution lambda = theta^3, rho = r^3, giving lambda = rho + 3 rho lambda^(2/3). He abandoned it, and a first attempt at the coefficients is struck out.
- He then solved by undetermined coefficients: theta = r + r^3 + r^5 + (2/3) r^7 + 0*r^9 - (2/3) r^11 - (7/9) r^13.
- He built the powers of theta:
  theta^2 = r^2 + 2r^4 + 3r^6 + 10/3 r^8 + 7/3 r^10 + 0*r^12 - 22/9 r^14
  theta^3 = r^3 + 3r^5 + 6r^7 + 9r^9 + 10r^11 + 7r^13
  theta^5 = r^5 + 5r^7 + 15r^9 + 100/3 r^11 + 175/3 r^13 + ...
  theta^7 = r^7 + 7r^9 + 28r^11 + 245/3 r^13
  theta^9 = r^9 + 9r^11 + 45 r^13
- A table of the contributions of theta, -theta^3/3, +theta^5/5, ..., +theta^13/13 to w/2 = arctan(theta) is summed column by column:
  w/2 = r + 2/3 r^3 + 1/5 r^5 - 10/21 r^7 - 8/9 r^9 - 14/33 r^11 + 113/117 r^13.
- Closed form: coefficient of r^m (m = 2n+1) = ((-1)^n/m) * Sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^k m(m-3)...(m-3k+3)/k! = ((-1)^n/m) * Sum_k C(m/3,k)(-3)^k. [Lagrange with theta = r(1+3theta^2)^(1/3), mine.]
- Back in q: w = q + q^3/6 + q^5/80 - 5/672 q^7 - q^9/288 - 7/16896 q^11 + 113/479232 q^13 ...
- Also log(w/q) = q^2/6 - q^4/720 - 181/22680 q^6.

(C) Numerics (left column). With rho = 206264.8 (log rho = 5.3144251, from 648000/pi on the previous page), Gauss forms the logarithms of the divisors that turn series (A) into arcseconds:
- 2 log rho + log 6 = 11.4070015
- 4 log rho + log 240 - log 13 = 22.5239684
- 6 log rho + log 2016 - log 43 = 33.5575727
- 8 log rho + log 20736 - log 191 = 44.5510927
- 10 log rho + log 114048 - log 479 = 55.5210035
He then evaluates p = 11 deg 6'40" = 40000". The successive terms are -250.714" (= 4'10.714"), +3.06430179", -0.04537818", +0.00073697", -0.00001264". Result: v = 11 deg 2' 32.30572217".
The previous page does the same with the coefficients of series (B), giving v near 168 deg, i.e. 180 deg - w.
errors: The first attempt at the theta series (with terms like 5/(2.3), 62/(2.3.4) r^11, +7/9 r^13) is wrong. Gauss himself struck it out; the rewritten series is correct.
The theta^5 r^15 coefficient is read in the transcription as 27; the correct value is 81. This term lies beyond the order used, so it has no effect. It may be a misreading.
The theta^9 r^13 coefficient is written ambiguously (46/45). The correct value is 45, and the summation table correctly uses 45/9 = 5.
All retained coefficients of v(p), theta(r), w/2(r), w(q) and log(w/q) check out, as do the numerical arcsecond terms. No substantive error found.

results.what: Inversion of Barker's equation 2tan(v/2)+(2/3)tan^3(v/2)=p into a power series for the true anomaly v, through p^11
results.modern_name: Series reversion of Barker's equation (parabolic Kepler problem)
results.usually_credited_to: Barker (1757) for the equation; series solutions are standard 18th-19th c. celestial mechanics (Lagrange, Euler)

results.what: Closed form for the general coefficient: (-1)^n/((2n+1)4^n) * Sum_{k<=n} C(2n+k,k) 3^-k
results.modern_name: Lagrange-Burmann inversion formula applied to Barker's equation

results.what: Expansion of v near 180 deg for large M: cot-form of Barker's equation, w = 180 deg - v = q + q^3/6 + q^5/80 - 5q^7/672 - ..., with q = 2(3M)^(-1/3), and general coefficient ((-1)^n/m) Sum_k C(m/3,k)(-3)^k
results.modern_name: Large-argument (asymptotic) series for parabolic true anomaly via Lagrange inversion
results.usually_credited_to: unsure (standard technique; specific series appears in 19th-c. tables for parabolic motion)

results.modern_name: Logarithmic form of the series for logarithmic computation

results.what: Logarithmic conversion of series coefficients to arcseconds and numerical evaluation for p = 40000"

deep.surprise_reason: Careful, correct application of Lagrange inversion to Barker's equation (the theme of a bundle labelled 'Lagrange 1816'). It includes neat closed binomial-sum coefficient formulas and an expansion valid near v = 180 deg. This is well within known Gauss interests (parabolic motion, Theoria Motus) and standard technique; it is a nice unpublished detail but not a new result.

checkable.asserts: closed binomial-sum formula for the coefficients of v(p)
